paras: The threatened lynching of Henry and Jennie Adcock took place at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, in September 1888, when threats were made to lynch the two white prisoners, who were charged with poisoning Henry Adcock's wife. Judge W. M. Shipp ordered them moved to the jail at Raleigh for safekeeping, and their trial was transferred to Vance County. No attack took place, and the trial was later postponed to February 1889.

Eliza Ann Adcock died of poison in Granville County on 31 July 1888, and her husband, Henry, and Jennie Adcock were charged with giving it to her. An exchange item in the Orange County Observer called Jennie 'his brother's wife', while the Richmond Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent later called her Henry's 'paramour'. The two were held in Oxford jail to be tried at the Granville Superior Court term in September, where the state chemist, H. B. Battle, was subpoenaed as a witness.

With the Granville court in session, Judge Shipp signed an order transferring the prisoners to Raleigh, stating that threats had been 'freely made' to lynch them if they remained in Oxford jail. The Durham Recorder said the judge acted knowing 'the feeling was very high' and the prisoners were in 'imminent danger'. The accused swore they could not get justice in Granville, and the case was removed to Vance County for trial at Henderson on 15 October.

On 12 September an officer took them through Henderson, and that night the Granville coroner delivered them, tied, to the Raleigh jail, where Deputy-Sheriff Johns locked them up under orders to guard them securely. According to the Dispatch's correspondent, the mob that had lynched three Black men the week before would also have lynched the Adcocks with more time, and threats continued at Oxford that they would not be allowed to live in Granville. The same correspondent later wrote that for 'the first week or more' at Raleigh the two were in 'hourly terror of lynching'.

On 15 October the Adcocks were taken from the Raleigh jail to Henderson for trial in Vance Superior Court. The case was put off to the next term, the February term of 1889, and the prisoners were returned to jail in the meantime. No report of the February trial or its outcome appears in the coverage.

The fullest coverage came from the Richmond Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent, whose 12 September telegram ran the transfer under the head 'Saved from Lynchers'. The correspondent reported the threats without comment but described the accused as 'dissolute and degraded people' and 'a very tough-looking pair', and in October as 'ignorant and degraded'. The Orange County Observer called the poisoning 'a black affair'.

North Carolina weeklies gave the case only short local notices: the Durham Recorder stressed the danger to the prisoners, and the Henderson Gold Leaf noted their passage under guard and said its people regretted that the case was to be tried there.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Henry and Jennie Adcock
bases: Two white prisoners charged with murder were moved out of Granville county by court order because of threats to lynch them; no attack was made, so this is a threatened lynching (A3, A4, A5).

No one was killed: the threats at Oxford against the prisoners, charged with poisoning, led to their removal to Raleigh and they were later taken to Henderson for trial (A3, A4, A5); the size of the threatening group is not given beyond 'the mob' and 'lynchers' (A3, A5).

The Richmond Dispatch's Raleigh telegram (A3) and the Durham Recorder's local item (A4) independently report the judge-ordered removal because of danger to the prisoners, and the Dispatch repeated it a month later (A5); the Gold Leaf confirms the transfer through Henderson (A2).

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondent of the Richmond Dispatch
accounts.gist: The prisoners were 'saved from lynchers' by Judge Shipp's transfer order, which cited threats to lynch them at Oxford; the correspondent added, on hearsay ('It is learned'), that the mob which lynched three Black men the week before would have lynched them with more time.

accounts.label: Durham Recorder local item
accounts.gist: Judge Shipp, knowing feeling was very high and the prisoners in imminent danger, ordered them removed to Raleigh until the Vance court term.

accounts.label: Henderson Gold Leaf
accounts.gist: The Adcocks passed through Henderson under an officer's charge for safe keeping at Raleigh; the case was later put off to the next term.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch reported the threats without comment under the head 'Saved from Lynchers' while describing the accused as 'dissolute and degraded' and 'a very tough-looking pair'.
North Carolina weeklies (Gold Leaf, Durham Recorder, Orange County Observer) ran short local items focused on the transfer and the court schedule.
